mcqs.question: Beyond scoring communication, why does silent coding also make it harder to arrive at a good solution efficiently?
options: It doesn't — silence has no effect on the outcome as long as the code is correct
It removes the interviewer's chance to redirect a wrong turn early, so a correction only happens after code is already written
Most interview platforms penalize typing without talking automatically
Silent candidates always run out of time before finishing
mcqs.explanation: Narration gives the interviewer a chance to nudge you off a wrong path while it's still cheap to change; without it, a wrong turn is only visible once it's already on the screen, which costs far more time to unwind. There's no platform penalty for silence itself, and running out of time isn't guaranteed either.

mcqs.question: In the "idea, why, then code" loop, why does the order matter?
options: It doesn't — explaining code right after writing it works just as well
Coding first prevents syntax errors, so it should always come before narration
Stating the idea before coding gives the interviewer a chance to catch a wrong turn before it's implemented; explaining afterward is just a post-hoc summary
The order only matters for optimal solutions, not brute-force ones
mcqs.explanation: Narrating first is what makes reasoning visible while it can still be corrected cheaply; narrating after the fact is retrospective and doesn't give the interviewer any chance to redirect. The order matters regardless of whether the approach is brute force or optimal.

mcqs.question: In the narrated two-pointer example, what makes the comment "moving left would only grow it further" valuable narration rather than filler?
options: It restates what the next line of code does
It states the invariant that justifies the decision to move the right pointer, which isn't visible just from reading the code
It's valuable mainly because it's phrased as a question
It describes the syntax of the while loop
mcqs.explanation: This sentence explains *why* moving right is the only valid move given the array is sorted — an invariant the interviewer can't get just by reading `right -= 1`. Restating what a line does or describing syntax is exactly the kind of narration this topic warns adds no value.

mcqs.question: What's the recommended filter for deciding what to narrate versus what to stay quiet on?
options: Narrate every line of code as you type it to maximize visible reasoning
Narrate decisions (data structure choice, why this loop bound, why reject an alternative); stay quiet on mechanics (naming, syntax, typo fixes)
Only narrate when the interviewer explicitly asks a question
Narrate only at the very start and the very end of the round
mcqs.explanation: Decisions carry the reasoning signal an interviewer needs; mechanics are already visible on screen and narrating them is filler that buries the signal. Narrating every line or only at the boundaries both miss the actual content that matters throughout the round.

mcqs.question: "This line checks if the list is empty" is an example of which narration mistake?
options: Narrating too infrequently
Narrating what the code does instead of why you chose to do it, which adds nothing the interviewer can't already see
Talking through the brute force unnecessarily
Answering an interruption without returning to the original thread
mcqs.explanation: This narrates something already visible on screen rather than the reasoning behind it — the useful version would explain why the empty case needs handling now, e.g. what it would otherwise break downstream. It isn't a frequency problem, a brute-force issue, or an interruption-handling issue.
